name: Weapon focus effect
statement: A witness who sees a weapon is said to remember the person holding it less well, and the claim holds up better for descriptions than for lineup identification.
meaning: The claim is about attention and memory, not fear. A weapon in the scene is held to draw looking time away from the perpetrator, so less of the perpetrator gets encoded. Two outcome measures are used to test this and they behave differently. The first is feature or description accuracy: what a witness can say afterwards about the perpetrator's face, build, hair and clothing. The second is identification accuracy: whether the witness picks the right person out of a lineup, and whether they pick an innocent person out of a lineup the perpetrator is absent from. Almost every popular account of weapon focus is describing the second measure, and the second measure is where the evidence is weakest. The cross-race effect entry covers the other main estimator variable in eyewitness identification, and the two are usually tested in the same archival datasets.

origin.who: Elizabeth F. Loftus, Geoffrey R. Loftus and Jane Messo
origin.note: 'Some facts about "weapon focus"' put subject-witnesses in front of slides of a fast-food restaurant. Half saw a customer point a gun at the cashier, half saw him hand over a cheque. The paper's own abstract calls the result 'the first direct empirical support for weapon focus', so the phenomenon was already named and argued about before this paper measured it.

evidence: Loftus, Loftus and Messo ran two experiments. Experiment 1 recorded eye movements and found more fixations on the gun than on the cheque, and longer ones. Experiment 2 found memory in the gun condition poorer than in the cheque condition. The abstract records that Experiment 1, the one with the eye-tracking, produced similar performance effects that were only marginally reliable. The article is paywalled and its fixation counts and durations could not be obtained. Steblay's meta-analysis pooled 19 tests. Its abstract reports a small effect of 0.13 for lineup identification and a moderate one of 0.55 for feature accuracy, and that is the split the whole literature has argued over since. Fawcett, Russell, Peace and Christie's meta-analysis is the large one. Its abstract gives an overall effect of weapon presence of g = 0.53, moderated by retention interval, exposure duration and threat, and not moderated by whether the event happened in a laboratory, a simulation or the real world. Kocab and Sporer's meta-analysis, run on person identifications and descriptions separately, found no reliable effect on correct identifications from target-present lineups, none on false identifications from target-absent lineups, and none on overall identification decisions. It found a medium effect on the accuracy of descriptions. It also found evidence of publication bias, which the other two did not.

replication.headline: Three meta-analyses support the effect and the two largest disagree about identification; five preregistered replications with 1,316 participants found nothing on either measure.
replication.detail: West, Mulligan and Bornstein set out to find moderators of the effect and could not produce the effect. They ran five preregistered experiments of 100 to 800 participants, total n = 1,316, using materials from studies that had previously shown it. Modality varied between videos and slides, weapon type between knife and gun, perpetrator gender, audio, and student against non-student samples. No experiment produced a reliable effect on description or on identification. Some produced reliable effects the other way, with better memory for armed perpetrators. Random-effects meta-analysis across all five gave Hedges' g = -0.138, 95% CI [-0.349, 0.073], p = 0.201, for target description, and an odds ratio of 0.841, 95% CI [0.541, 1.307], p = 0.440, for lineup identification. Their manipulation worked: threat ratings differed by an average d = 0.774 without the memory effect following. Körner, Faul and Nuthmann tested the attention account directly with eye-tracking, using stimuli built from a United States study that had reported large memory effects. Weapon presence did not reduce recall of the perpetrator's appearance in any of three experiments. Their Bayes factors favoured absence: BF01 = 4.0 with 68 participants viewing videos, 5.9 with 56 viewing slide shows, and 19.0 with 266 online. In Experiment 2 the gun did attract more gaze than the phone, and it did not cost viewing time on the perpetrator, which is the step the attention-shift account needs.

study.cite: West, J. T., Mulligan, N. W., & Bornstein, B. H. (2026). Four (and a half) preregistered failures to replicate the weapon focus effect in online samples. Psychology, Public Policy, and Law, 32(1), 48-64.

replicated.weighting: random-effects across five experiments, target description

limits: The effect thins out wherever real crimes are involved. Valentine, Pickering and Darling analysed 640 identification attempts across 314 lineups run by the Metropolitan Police in London. Their abstract reports no independent, statistically reliable effect of weapon focus, and the same null for cross-race identification and for delay. Erickson and colleagues, writing on facial composites, put it that surveys of real cases show a weaker effect of weapon presence than of other factors such as perpetrator race and duration of encoding. Mansour, Hamilton and Gibson list Tollestrup and colleagues, Valentine and colleagues, and Yuille and Tollestrup as field analyses in which the effect was absent. Behrman and Davey's 271 police cases produced no reliable difference in lineup identification between weapon and no-weapon crimes, as Hatfield's review describes them. Tollestrup and colleagues are the archival exception. Hatfield reports 44% of identification attempts producing a positive identification in weapon crimes against 71% without a weapon. He reports the confound in the same breath. Police ran lineups in 51% of weapon offences and 23% of weaponless ones, so the two rates come from differently selected witnesses. Fawcett's abstract says the opposite about setting, reporting that laboratory, simulation and real-world events did not differ. Whether the archival record contains the effect is therefore an open disagreement between a meta-analysis and the individual studies it pooled, and this entry could not read the meta-analysis to see how it was resolved. Three of the four figures a reader would most want are behind paywalls with no repository copy: Loftus, Loftus and Messo's article, Steblay's, and Fawcett's. Their abstracts were read at Crossref, at OpenAlex and at the colab.ws index, which reproduces publisher abstracts, and nothing here rests on their bodies. Fawcett's separate estimate for feature accuracy could not be obtained from any source fetched for this entry, so only the overall 0.53 and the identification figure appear. The identification figure, g = 0.22 for laboratory studies, is quoted from Carlson and colleagues' description of it, reached through Semantic Scholar's citation index rather than the article. It is kept out of the structured fields for that reason. Archival counts from Tollestrup and colleagues and from Behrman and Davey are quoted here from Hatfield's undergraduate literature review, the only fetchable source located for them. No multi-laboratory preregistered replication exists. West and colleagues' five experiments were all online, and the authors allow that the effect may be real and dependent on methodological factors such as study modality.
misreadings: Two measures get treated as one. Steblay's pooled 0.13 for lineup identification and 0.55 for feature accuracy are not two estimates of the same thing, and Kocab and Sporer found the identification effect absent while the description effect held. A witness who cannot describe a robber well is a different problem from a witness who picks the wrong man, and only the second convicts anybody. The famous eye-tracking result is smaller than its reputation. Loftus, Loftus and Messo's Experiment 1 is the one everyone cites for the gaze data, and its own abstract records the memory effects there as marginal. Threat is assumed to be the mechanism and the direct tests point elsewhere. Pickel crossed threat against unusualness in two experiments and found description accuracy affected by unusualness and not by threat. Mansour and colleagues note that a gun in a context where it belongs, such as a shooting range, produces no effect. Fawcett's meta-analysis found weapons produced numerically but not reliably greater impairment than other unusual objects, as Carlson and colleagues describe it. Legal recognition runs ahead of the field evidence rather than with it. New Jersey's model criminal jury charge on identification, revised in May 2020, instructs jurors to consider whether the witness saw a weapon, citing State v. Henderson at 262-63. Seale-Carlisle and colleagues surveyed 76 eyewitness experts in 2020 and 2021 and 80% agreed that seeing a weapon can later affect identification performance. Fawcett, Peace and Greve wrote in 2016 that testimony on weapon focus is rarely admissible in court and argued it was robust enough to guide practice. West and colleagues, a decade later, say their results call that consensus into question. Every part of that recognition tracks the laboratory literature on identification, which is the part of the literature that has failed to replicate.

sources.text: Loftus, E. F., Loftus, G. R., & Messo, J. (1987). Some facts about "weapon focus". Law and Human Behavior, 11(1), 55-62. Paywalled with no repository copy; the abstract was read at the colab.ws index, which reproduces the publisher's. The fixation counts and durations quoted in secondary accounts were not verified and do not appear here.

Steblay, N. M. (1992). A meta-analytic review of the weapon focus effect. Law and Human Behavior, 16(4), 413-424. Paywalled and not read. The 19 tests, the 0.13 for lineup identification and the 0.55 for feature accuracy come from the abstract, read at colab.ws.

Fawcett, J. M., Russell, E. J., Peace, K. A., & Christie, J. (2013). Of guns and geese: A meta-analytic review of the 'weapon focus' literature. Psychology, Crime & Law, 19(1), 35-66. Paywalled and not read. Metadata verified at Crossref; the overall g = 0.53 and the moderators come from the publisher abstract as reproduced by OpenAlex.

Kocab, K., & Sporer, S. L. (2016). The weapon focus effect for person identifications and descriptions: A meta-analysis. In Advances in Psychology and Law (pp. 71-117). Springer. Paywalled and not read; the abstract was read at colab.ws. Source for the null results on identification, the medium effect on descriptions and the publication bias.

West, J. T., Mulligan, N. W., & Bornstein, B. H. (2026). Four (and a half) preregistered failures to replicate the weapon focus effect in online samples. Psychology, Public Policy, and Law, 32(1), 48-64. Full text read at PubMed Central. Crossref gives the version of record as 2026; the PMC copy carries 2025.

Körner, H. M., Faul, F., & Nuthmann, A. (2023). Revisiting the role of attention in the 'weapon focus effect': Do weapons draw gaze away from the perpetrator under naturalistic viewing conditions? Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, 85(6), 1868-1887. Full text read at PubMed Central.

Mansour, J. K., Hamilton, C. M., & Gibson, M. T. (2019). Understanding the weapon focus effect: The role of threat, unusualness, exposure duration, and scene complexity. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 33(6), 991-1007. Accepted manuscript read in full at Queen Margaret University's repository.

Pickel, K. L. (1998). Unusualness and threat as possible causes of 'weapon focus'. Memory, 6(3), 277-295. Abstract read at colab.ws; the source for description accuracy being affected by unusualness and not by threat.

Valentine, T., Pickering, A., & Darling, S. (2003). Characteristics of eyewitness identification that predict the outcome of real lineups. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 17(8), 969-993. Abstract read; the source for the field null across 640 identification attempts in 314 real lineups.

Fawcett, J. M., Peace, K. A., & Greve, A. (2016). Looking down the barrel of a gun: What do we know about the weapon focus effect? Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition, 5(3), 257-263. Blocked by the publisher and not read; the abstract was read at Semantic Scholar, and it is the source for the claim that such testimony is rarely admissible.

Seale-Carlisle, T. M., Quigley-McBride, A., Teitcher, J., Crozier, W., Dodson, C. S., & Garrett, B. L. (2024). New insights on expert opinion about eyewitness memory research. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 20(5), 903-924. Read at PubMed Central; the source for 80% of 76 experts agreeing about weapon presence.

New Jersey Courts. Model criminal jury charge, 'Identification: in-court and out-of-court identifications', revised 5/18/2020. Section (c) is headed Weapon Focus and cites State v. Henderson, 208 N.J. at 262-63. Read in full.

Erickson, W. B., Brown, C., Portch, E., Lampinen, J. M., Marsh, J. E., Fodarella, C., Petkovic, A., Coultas, C., Newby, A., Date, L., Hancock, P. J. B., & Frowd, C. D. (2022). The impact of weapons and unusual objects on the construction of facial composites. Psychology, Crime & Law, 30(3), 207-228. Open-access copy read in full at White Rose eprints; the source for real-case surveys showing a weaker weapon effect than perpetrator race or encoding duration.

Carlson, C. A., Pleasant, W. E., Weatherford, D. R., Carlson, M. A., & Bednarz, J. E. (2016). The weapon focus effect: Testing an extension of the unusualness hypothesis. Applied Psychology in Criminal Justice, 12(2). PDF read in full. Source for Fawcett's finding that weapons impaired memory numerically but not reliably more than other unusual objects, and for the 963 undergraduates in which only the handgun reduced identification accuracy.

Carlson, C. A., Young, D. F., Weatherford, D. R., Carlson, M. A., Bednarz, J. E., & Jones, A. R. (2016). The influence of perpetrator exposure time and weapon presence/timing on eyewitness confidence and accuracy. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 30(6), 898-910. Not read. Its sentence giving Fawcett's laboratory identification estimate as g = 0.22 was obtained through Semantic Scholar's citation-context index.

Hatfield, T. Weapon focus effect: A literature review. Afficio Undergraduate Journal, Saint Mary's University. An undergraduate review, read in full, and the only fetchable source located for the archival counts attributed here to Tollestrup and colleagues and to Behrman and Davey.
